Backpressure in a streaming pipeline is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

## Common Implementations

The source describes three primary approaches:

1. **Bounded queues** — A fixed-size buffer between producer and consumer. When the queue becomes full, the producer is blocked from adding more items until the consumer drains some data. This is the simplest form of backpressure and is commonly found in traditional thread-based systems.

2. **Credit-based flow control** — The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items (credits). As items are processed, credits are consumed; when credits run low, the consumer grants more, giving the producer explicit control signals rather than implicit blocking.

3. **Reactive-pull models** — Inverts the traditional push model: instead of the producer deciding when to emit, the consumer requests items on its own schedule. This is common in reactive streams and pull-based systems where the consumer entirely controls the rate of data flow.

## Significance

Backpressure prevents a cascading failure mode in distributed or multi-component pipelines: if any downstream stage slows down, proper backpressure ensures the entire pipeline slows gracefully rather than allowing fast upstream stages to exhaust system resources (memory, CPU, file handles) by accumulating unprocessed data.
